title: This Arctic Town Is Moving Away From Its Own Mine
question: Why do people live in Kiruna?
message: This video tells curious adults that Kiruna exists because iron ore reported to the Swedish state back in 1736 only became worth mining once a railway could carry it over the mountains to an ice-free Norwegian harbour, and that its people now move the town itself, rather than leave, as the mine swallows the ground beneath it.
angle: People live in Kiruna because iron ore known since at least 1736 became worth mining once a railway could carry it over the mountains to Narvik's ice-free harbour, and because the mine still supplies most of the EU's iron ore and pays for the town to move rather than die, despite the mine swallowing the old centre, a blast under their feet every night, about three weeks without sunrise, a new centre that can be colder than the old one, and a move that costs residents their streets and squeezes the last reindeer route of a Sámi herding community.
ghi_chu_khung: Bản viết lại 28/11/2026 (bản 22/11 lưu ở script.v2.json). Khung tập 6 (khác tập 5): mở ở bàn với chìa khoá phòng thuê (cảnh 1), vẫn ở bàn cho lời hứa, thẻ hộ chiếu lật vào đúng chữ 'Kiruna' (cảnh 2) → chuyến đi theo bốn lần tới: tháng 2 (3–7), tháng 8/2025 đi theo nhà thờ (8–11), tháng 12/2025 và tháng 6/2026 (12–13) → về bàn cho chương nghiêm (14), hồi ức lối tuần lộc không gag (15) → outro ở bàn: Wob bật/tắt đèn bàn trên chìa khoá để kể hai mùa, đóng dấu dưới đèn, treo chìa khoá lên đinh hướng đông (tập 5: đọc bưu thiếp rồi đóng dấu; tập 4: đóng dấu trước rồi nói lý do) → đuôi ở kệ. Wob đổi ý bằng đồ vật: chìa khoá vào chùm chìa nhà (cảnh 2, định chuyển tới) → tháo ra bỏ túi (cảnh 4, sau nổ mìn và động đất) → đeo lại (cảnh 9, sau Great Church Walk) → cất ngăn kéo (cảnh 12, tháng 12) → lấy ra ngắm nhưng không đeo (cảnh 13) → treo đinh (outro, SUMMER ONLY). Không 'I changed my mind', không tóm ba vế, không 'Would I move there?', không cặp 'It suits / It does not suit', không chương theo mốc giờ. Lời giải Narvik/ice-free ở cảnh 6, sau hai giả thuyết sai (cực quang/du lịch, Icehotel); map-kiruna-rail chỉ xuất hiện từ cảnh 6. Trang phục Wob trong chuyến đi: ba lô to, khăn len (mùa đông), kính râm (hè); ở bàn: đồ ở nhà. Ảnh AI: không dùng; shots chỉ trỏ 3 bản đồ code + thẻ chữ, mọi cảnh vẽ theo y_hinh. Người thật (Mangi, Lundbohm, nhà vua, Kuhmunen, Moström) không vẽ mặt: người que, vật tượng trưng hoặc thẻ chữ.

scenes.narration: The town is Kiruna, in the far north of Sweden, above the Arctic Circle. Under the hill next door is an iron mine, and it is slowly swallowing the ground the old centre stood on. So the town is packing up and moving east. Houses, shops, a clock tower, even a big red wooden church. I went there to move in. I even put the key on my own key ring, next to my house keys. But one small fact kept bugging me. In seventeen thirty-six, a Sámi man named Amund Amundson Mangi reported the iron ore here to the Swedish state. He got a reward, and no taxes for life. The town didn't start until nineteen hundred. So what was everyone waiting for? My first guesses were terrible. Both of them.

scenes.narration: I arrived on a February evening and rented that room in the old centre. A bed, a radiator, a glass of water on the nightstand. At a quarter past one in the morning, the glass started to hum. Then it shuffled a little to the left. I lay very still. So did the radiator. The mine blasts every night, between one fifteen and one forty-five. The blasting area is cleared first, and the tunnels are aired out for a few hours afterwards. Up on the surface, the ground sometimes shivers. My glass shivered right on schedule. By the third night, I was awake before it started, just to be polite. The glass and I had an understanding.

scenes.narration: The next day I took the mine tour, into the mountain next to town. According to LKAB, the state-owned company that runs it, this is the world's largest underground iron ore mine. Its main haulage level sits about one thousand three hundred and sixty-five metres down. That's nearly four and a half thousand feet. They take the ore out from below, level by level, and let the rock above cave in behind them. Think of an hourglass. Pull sand from the bottom, and the top of the pile slowly sinks. Kiruna's old centre is the top of the pile. And the ore body keeps running east, under the town. In May twenty twenty, the mine set off the biggest mining-induced earthquake ever recorded in Sweden. Magnitude four point one. Nobody was hurt. That night I slid the key off my key ring and put it in my pocket. Pockets are for maybes.

scenes.narration: So, back to all that waiting. My first guess was the sky. I stood outside one night with a flask of tea, waiting for proof. The northern lights came out, green and slow. My nose went numb. Lovely. And wrong. Tourism is big here now. In twenty twenty-four, Kiruna had a record year, with more than six hundred thousand commercial guest nights. But the town came first, and the tourists followed. My second guess was the hotel made of ice, in the village of Jukkasjärvi, about seventeen kilometres away. That's roughly eleven miles. I sat on an ice bed in my coat to think it over. Icehotel began as an ice-sculpture workshop in nineteen eighty-nine. That's eighty-nine years after the town. Wrong again. My bottom agreed.

scenes.narration: The real answer rolled past me at a level crossing on the way back. An ore train. Up to sixty-eight wagons, about seven hundred and fifty metres long. Roughly seven football pitches of iron. I started counting wagons and lost count. Twice. First, the ore had a flaw. It is rich in phosphorus, and in older furnaces that made the iron brittle. In the eighteen-seventies, a new method, the Thomas process, turned that flaw into a selling point. That left the bigger problem. Iron is no use inside a mountain. It has to reach the sea. Sweden's own coast is to the east, at Luleå, on the Gulf of Bothnia. That sea is iced up for five to six months a year. A port like that is a shop whose front door freezes shut every winter. So they ran a railway the other way, over the mountains, to Narvik on the Norwegian coast. Warm water from the Gulf Stream keeps Narvik's harbour ice-free all year. The line reached Kiruna around nineteen hundred and was joined up to Narvik in nineteen oh two. The king opened it officially in nineteen oh three. Today, about twelve loaded trains a day still run from Kiruna to Narvik. Luleå ships ore too, with icebreakers helping in winter. The iron had been waiting for a door that opens in January.

scenes.narration: Then the town could happen. Kiruna counts nineteen hundred as its birth year, when the king approved its town plan. The mining company's first managing director, a geologist called Hjalmar Lundbohm, wanted a model town. He brought in a leading planner to fit the streets to the climate. By nineteen ten, about seven thousand five hundred people lived here. At the end of twenty twenty-five, the municipality had about twenty-two thousand four hundred. They're spread over land slightly bigger than New Jersey. And the mine still matters far beyond the town. LKAB says it produces more than eighty percent of the iron ore mined in the European Union. I stood by the tracks with the key in my pocket. The train was still going past.

scenes.narration: I went back that August, because a church was going for a walk. Kiruna Church is big, red and wooden, finished in nineteen twelve, and much loved. The mine needed its ground. So on the nineteenth and twentieth of August, twenty twenty-five, it rolled about five kilometres to the new centre, in one piece. It rode on remote-controlled trailers with more than two hundred wheels. LKAB put its weight at about six hundred and seventy tonnes. To make room, the road was widened from nine metres to twenty-four, which took a year, according to LKAB. A year of roadworks, for a trip of two days. My plan was simple. Walk beside the church, all the way. I overtook it almost at once. I stopped. I waited. I overtook it again. It was slower than a slow walk. I tried walking backwards. Still too fast.

scenes.narration: That December, I went back for the dark. In Kiruna, the sun stays below the horizon from about the eleventh of December to the first of January. That's about three weeks without a sunrise. At noon, the sky went pink at the edges, then gave up. January averages about minus eleven Celsius. That's around twelve Fahrenheit. And the new centre has a problem of its own. According to a University of Gothenburg study, winter temperatures there can be up to ten degrees Celsius lower than at the old site. Cold air pools in the dip where it was built, the way water fills a bowl. Narrow streets and tall blocks keep the low sun off the pavement. On the new square, the wind found me in seconds. The town's North Sámi name is Giron. It comes from the mountain, and giron means rock ptarmigan, a small bird that turns white in winter. I would have liked to turn white and stop caring. Instead I went back to my room, slid the key off my key ring again, and put it in a drawer.

scenes.narration: North of town, behind the mountain Luossavaara, runs a reindeer route. Gabna, a Sámi reindeer herding community, moves its herds this way between summer and winter grazing land. Their old route along the lake was cut off by the mine and the town. Now LKAB plans a rare earth mine called Per Geijer, right on the route that is left. LKAB calls it one of the largest rare earth deposits in Europe, and the EU lists it as a strategic project. The company argues that electric cars need the magnets these metals go into. Gabna's chair, Lars-Marcus Kuhmunen, has said there is nowhere left for them to move. LKAB's chief executive, Jan Moström, has said the problem is that both sides need the same land. Gabna has asked the European Court of Human Rights to look at the case. In December twenty twenty-five, it ended its cooperation agreement with LKAB, saying consultations had changed nothing. scenes.narration: The key lives under my desk lamp now. Lamp on. That's June. Sun at midnight, a church you can walk beside, a cinnamon bun at the roadside. Lamp off. That's December. Weeks without a sunrise, and a new square that holds the cold. Lamp on again. I'm not made of stone. Kiruna didn't come here for the weather. It came for the iron, and when the iron started pulling the ground away, the town picked up its church and kept going. I admire that a lot. I just can't do the dark. Summer only. I'd come every June, help carry something heavy, and leave before the sun does. If you like snow, quiet and a project measured in decades, you'd outlast me easily. I hung the key on a nail by my window, pointing east, in case its door turns up. Would you move your whole town to keep your job?

claims.quote: The town is Kiruna, in the far north of Sweden, above the Arctic Circle.
claims.statement: Kiruna is a town in Norrbotten County in the far north of Sweden, located north of the Arctic Circle.

claims.quote: Under the hill next door is an iron mine, and it is slowly swallowing the ground the old centre stood on. So the town is packing up and moving east.
claims.statement: LKAB's underground iron ore mine in Kiirunavaara, next to Kiruna, causes ground deformation that spreads toward the town, so Kiruna's old centre is being dismantled and the centre relocated about 3 km to the east.

claims.quote: Houses, shops, a clock tower, even a big red wooden church.
claims.statement: Kiruna's urban transformation involves replacing or moving homes and shops, moving the old town hall's clock tower to the new centre, and moving the large red wooden Kiruna Church (moved in August 2025).

claims.quote: In seventeen thirty-six, a Sámi man named Amund Amundson Mangi reported the iron ore here to the Swedish state. He got a reward, and no taxes for life.
claims.statement: According to LKAB's company history, in 1736 a Sámi man named Amund Amundson Mangi reported the iron ore deposits in the Kiruna area to the Swedish state, and was rewarded with money and exemption from taxes for life.

claims.quote: The town didn't start until nineteen hundred.
claims.statement: Kiruna counts 1900 as its founding year, the year the King approved its town plan.

claims.quote: The mine blasts every night, between one fifteen and one forty-five. The blasting area is cleared first, and the tunnels are aired out for a few hours afterwards. Up on the surface, the ground sometimes shivers.
claims.statement: LKAB's Kiruna mine carries out its production blasting every night between 01:15 and 01:45; the blasting area is evacuated beforehand, the mine is ventilated for a few hours afterwards, and vibrations can sometimes be felt above ground.

claims.quote: According to LKAB, the state-owned company that runs it, this is the world's largest underground iron ore mine.
claims.statement: LKAB, the Swedish state-owned mining company that operates the Kiruna mine, describes it as the world's largest underground iron ore mine (a description from LKAB itself, not independently confirmed).

claims.quote: Its main haulage level sits about one thousand three hundred and sixty-five metres down. That's nearly four and a half thousand feet.
claims.statement: The current main haulage level of LKAB's Kiruna mine is at a depth of 1,365 metres (about 4,480 feet).

claims.quote: They take the ore out from below, level by level, and let the rock above cave in behind them. Think of an hourglass. Pull sand from the bottom, and the top of the pile slowly sinks.
claims.statement: LKAB mines Kiruna using sublevel caving: ore is extracted level by level and the overlying waste rock caves in to fill the space, so no large voids remain underground but the ground surface above gradually subsides.

claims.quote: And the ore body keeps running east, under the town.
claims.statement: The Kiruna ore body continues eastward beneath the old town (and northward), so ground deformation from mining continues to spread toward the town.

claims.quote: In May twenty twenty, the mine set off the biggest mining-induced earthquake ever recorded in Sweden. Magnitude four point one. Nobody was hurt.
claims.statement: On 18 May 2020 a magnitude 4.1 (ML, Swedish National Seismic Network) seismic event occurred at LKAB's Kiruna mine, the largest mining-induced earthquake recorded in Sweden; no one among the people in the mine was injured.

claims.quote: In twenty twenty-four, Kiruna had a record year, with more than six hundred thousand commercial guest nights.
claims.statement: Kiruna recorded 607,818 commercial guest nights in 2024, a record for the municipality.

claims.quote: My second guess was the hotel made of ice, in the village of Jukkasjärvi, about seventeen kilometres away. That's roughly eleven miles.
claims.statement: Icehotel is located in the village of Jukkasjärvi, about 17 km (about 11 miles) from Kiruna.

claims.quote: Icehotel began as an ice-sculpture workshop in nineteen eighty-nine. That's eighty-nine years after the town.
claims.statement: Icehotel in Jukkasjärvi began in 1989 as an ice-sculpture workshop, 89 years after Kiruna's founding year of 1900.

claims.quote: Up to sixty-eight wagons, about seven hundred and fifty metres long. Roughly seven football pitches of iron.
claims.statement: Iron ore trains on the Malmbanan line between Kiruna and Narvik run with up to 68 wagons and are about 750 m long, roughly the length of seven 105-metre football pitches.

claims.quote: Sweden's own coast is to the east, at Luleå, on the Gulf of Bothnia. That sea is iced up for five to six months a year.
claims.statement: Luleå, Sweden's ore port on the Gulf of Bothnia east of Kiruna, lies in waters that are covered by ice for about five to six months each year.

claims.quote: So they ran a railway the other way, over the mountains, to Narvik on the Norwegian coast. Warm water from the Gulf Stream keeps Narvik's harbour ice-free all year.
claims.statement: The ore railway from Kiruna was built west over the mountains to the port of Narvik on the Norwegian coast, which LKAB says stays ice-free all year thanks to the warm Gulf Stream.

claims.quote: The line reached Kiruna around nineteen hundred and was joined up to Narvik in nineteen oh two. The king opened it officially in nineteen oh three.
claims.statement: The railway reached Kiruna around 1900, the line to Narvik was completed in 1902, and it was officially inaugurated by King Oscar II in 1903.

claims.quote: Today, about twelve loaded trains a day still run from Kiruna to Narvik. Luleå ships ore too, with icebreakers helping in winter.
claims.statement: According to Trafikverket, about 12 loaded ore trains a day run from Kiruna to Narvik; Luleå remains an LKAB ore port, and winter shipping there relies on icebreaker assistance.

claims.quote: Kiruna counts nineteen hundred as its birth year, when the king approved its town plan.
claims.statement: Kiruna considers 1900 its year of birth, when the King approved the town plan.

claims.quote: The mining company's first managing director, a geologist called Hjalmar Lundbohm, wanted a model town. He brought in a leading planner to fit the streets to the climate.
claims.statement: Hjalmar Lundbohm, a geologist who became LKAB's first managing director, wanted Kiruna to be a model community and engaged a leading town planner (Per-Olov Hallman) to design a plan adapted to the climate.

claims.quote: By nineteen ten, about seven thousand five hundred people lived here.
claims.statement: Kiruna had about 7,500 inhabitants in 1910.

claims.quote: At the end of twenty twenty-five, the municipality had about twenty-two thousand four hundred. They're spread over land slightly bigger than New Jersey.
claims.statement: Kiruna Municipality had 22,402 inhabitants on 31 December 2025 (Statistics Sweden), and its land area of 19,307 km² is slightly larger than the land area of the US state of New Jersey (about 19,049 km², 2020 Census).

claims.quote: LKAB says it produces more than eighty percent of the iron ore mined in the European Union.
claims.statement: LKAB states that it produces more than 80 percent of the iron ore mined in the European Union (86 percent in 2025, per its annual report).

claims.quote: Kiruna Church is big, red and wooden, finished in nineteen twelve, and much loved.
claims.statement: Kiruna Church is a large red wooden church completed in 1912 and is one of the town's best-loved buildings.

claims.quote: So on the nineteenth and twentieth of August, twenty twenty-five, it rolled about five kilometres to the new centre, in one piece. It rode on remote-controlled trailers with more than two hundred wheels.
claims.statement: On 19 and 20 August 2025 Kiruna Church was moved in one piece about 5 km to the new city centre on remote-controlled self-propelled trailers with more than 200 wheels.

claims.quote: LKAB put its weight at about six hundred and seventy tonnes.
claims.statement: LKAB gave the weight of Kiruna Church as about 672 tonnes; the Church of Sweden gives about 600 tonnes.

claims.quote: To make room, the road was widened from nine metres to twenty-four, which took a year, according to LKAB. A year of roadworks, for a trip of two days.
claims.statement: To move Kiruna Church, the road was widened from 9 to 24 metres, work that took about a year according to LKAB, for a move that took two days.

claims.quote: Swedish television showed the whole move live. AP called the broadcast The Great Church Walk, and it even had a fika break each day.
claims.statement: Swedish public broadcaster SVT broadcast the whole church move live; the Associated Press described the broadcast as 'The Great Church Walk', with a daily fika (coffee) break.

claims.quote: Thousands of people lined the route. The king came too.
claims.statement: Thousands of people watched the Kiruna Church move along the route, and King Carl XVI Gustaf attended.

claims.quote: At its new spot, the church was turned around a hundred and eighty degrees, so it still faces the town.
claims.statement: At its new site Kiruna Church was rotated 180 degrees, so that its front still faces the town.

claims.quote: It's still closed for now. The parish expects to reopen it in twenty twenty-seven.
claims.statement: As of November 2026 Kiruna Church remains closed after the move; the Church of Sweden's Kiruna parish expects to reopen it in 2027.

claims.quote: Eight days after the church parked, LKAB presented a new forecast. About six thousand more people and around two thousand seven hundred more homes would have to move, over roughly the next ten years.
claims.statement: On 28 August 2025, eight days after Kiruna Church reached its new site on 20 August, LKAB presented a new ground-deformation forecast under which about 6,000 more people and about 2,700 more homes in Kiruna would be affected and need to be compensated over the next ten years.

claims.quote: Altogether, according to LKAB, the move now affects about twelve thousand people and around five thousand four hundred homes. That's roughly two thirds of the town.
claims.statement: According to LKAB, Kiruna's urban transformation now affects about 12,000 people and about 5,400 homes in total, roughly two thirds of the town.

claims.quote: Homeowners get a choice. LKAB can build them an equivalent new home. Or it pays the market value plus twenty-five percent, set by an independent valuer.
claims.statement: Kiruna homeowners affected by the mine can choose an equivalent replacement home built by LKAB or a payment of the market value plus 25 percent, assessed by an independent certified valuer.

claims.quote: I walked east, about three kilometres, to where everyone was going.
claims.statement: Kiruna's new city centre lies about 3 km east of the old centre.

claims.quote: The new centre opened in September twenty twenty-two, with a three-day party.
claims.statement: Kiruna's new city centre was inaugurated with a three-day festival on 1 to 3 September 2022.

claims.quote: The new town hall is a round building called Kristallen, the Crystal. It opened back in late twenty eighteen.
claims.statement: Kiruna's new town hall, Kristallen ('The Crystal'), designed by Henning Larsen, is a round building that opened in November 2018.

claims.quote: Next to it stands the old town hall's clock tower, moved across from the old centre.
claims.statement: The clock tower of Kiruna's old town hall was moved to the new centre and stands beside the new town hall, Kristallen.

claims.quote: In Kiruna, the sun stays below the horizon from about the eleventh of December to the first of January. That's about three weeks without a sunrise.
claims.statement: In Kiruna the polar night, when the sun does not rise above the horizon, lasts from about 11 December to 1 January, roughly three weeks (exact dates vary by a day or two with terrain).

claims.quote: January averages about minus eleven Celsius. That's around twelve Fahrenheit.
claims.statement: Kiruna's average January temperature is about minus 11 °C (−11.3 °C, about 12 °F) according to SMHI's 1991–2020 normals for Kiruna Airport.

claims.quote: According to a University of Gothenburg study, winter temperatures there can be up to ten degrees Celsius lower than at the old site. Cold air pools in the dip where it was built, the way water fills a bowl. Narrow streets and tall blocks keep the low sun off the pavement.
claims.statement: A University of Gothenburg study (Jennie Sjöholm, Urban Design International, 2025) found that winter temperatures in Kiruna's new centre can be up to 10 °C lower than at the old centre, because it lies in a hollow where cold air collects and its narrow streets and tall buildings block the low winter sun.

claims.quote: The town's North Sámi name is Giron. It comes from the mountain, and giron means rock ptarmigan, a small bird that turns white in winter.
claims.statement: Kiruna's North Sámi name is Giron, from the mountain Gironvárri (Kiirunavaara); giron means rock ptarmigan, a bird whose plumage turns white in winter.

claims.quote: From late May to mid-July, about seven weeks, the sun doesn't set here at all.
claims.statement: In Kiruna the midnight sun lasts from about late May to mid-July, roughly seven weeks, during which the sun does not set.

claims.quote: July averages about thirteen Celsius.
claims.statement: Kiruna's average July temperature is about 13 °C (13.2 °C) according to SMHI's 1991–2020 normals for Kiruna Airport.

claims.quote: On average, the last spring frost comes around the first of June, and the first autumn frost around the fourth of September.
claims.statement: According to SMHI's 1991–2020 normals for Kiruna, the last spring frost occurs on average around 1 June and the first autumn frost around 4 September.

claims.quote: Most of the old houses are not moved. They are demolished, and for many people the streets they grew up on are simply gone.
claims.statement: Most buildings in Kiruna's old centre are demolished and replaced rather than moved, and many residents are unhappy at losing the streets they grew up in.

claims.quote: In October twenty twenty-three, the tall blocks that made the old skyline came down.
claims.statement: In October 2023 the tall apartment blocks by architect Ralph Erskine that formed Kiruna's classic skyline in the old centre were demolished.

claims.quote: In December twenty twenty-five, renters in one neighbourhood started a petition saying their compensation was not enough.
claims.statement: In December 2025 tenants in Kiruna's Thule neighbourhood started a petition arguing that the compensation offered for the move was not enough.

claims.quote: Gabna, a Sámi reindeer herding community, moves its herds this way between summer and winter grazing land. Their old route along the lake was cut off by the mine and the town.
claims.statement: Gabna, a Sámi reindeer herding community (sameby) near Kiruna, moves its reindeer between summer and winter pastures through the area north of the town; its former route along Lake Luossajärvi was blocked by the mine and the town, and the herds now pass behind the mountain Luossavaara.

claims.quote: Now LKAB plans a rare earth mine called Per Geijer, right on the route that is left.
claims.statement: LKAB's planned Per Geijer rare earth and iron deposit lies on the migration route that Gabna's reindeer still use behind Luossavaara.

claims.quote: LKAB calls it one of the largest rare earth deposits in Europe, and the EU lists it as a strategic project.
claims.statement: LKAB describes Per Geijer as one of the largest rare earth deposits in Europe, and the EU has designated it a strategic project under the Critical Raw Materials Act.

claims.quote: The company argues that electric cars need the magnets these metals go into.
claims.statement: LKAB argues that rare earth elements from Per Geijer are needed for the permanent magnets used in electric vehicles.

claims.quote: Gabna's chair, Lars-Marcus Kuhmunen, has said there is nowhere left for them to move. LKAB's chief executive, Jan Moström, has said the problem is that both sides need the same land.
claims.statement: Gabna's chair Lars-Marcus Kuhmunen has said the community has nowhere left to move, while LKAB chief executive Jan Moström has said the problem is that both parties need the same land (TT, July 2025).

claims.quote: Gabna has asked the European Court of Human Rights to look at the case.
claims.statement: Gabna reindeer herding community has asked the European Court of Human Rights to examine its case over the land affected by LKAB's mining plans.

claims.quote: In December twenty twenty-five, it ended its cooperation agreement with LKAB, saying consultations had changed nothing. LKAB said it would look for a new way to talk.
claims.statement: On 1 December 2025 Gabna ended its cooperation agreement with LKAB, saying consultations had not changed any mining decisions; LKAB responded that it would seek a new form of dialogue.

claims.quote: It is rich in phosphorus, and in older furnaces that made the iron brittle. In the eighteen-seventies, a new method, the Thomas process, turned that flaw into a selling point.
claims.statement: The Kiruna-area iron ore is rich in phosphorus, which made iron brittle in older production processes; after the Thomas process was invented in the 1870s, phosphorus-rich ore became valuable, one reason the Swedish ore fields became profitable to mine.
